summary: Experimental document on synchronizing service boundaries and mapping elements between servers using the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol. LoST maps a location to a service, such as the right emergency call center. This keeps the servers' data consistent.

eli5.summary: A map says which fire station covers which streets. This memo helps map-keeping computers copy updated boundaries from each other so they all agree.

questions: how to sync lost mapping data
how do lost servers synchronize mappings
subtitle: How emergency-call location servers copy service-area maps to each other.

tldr.problem: Emergency calls should be routed to the nearest Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP), so servers need to share the service boundaries that say which area maps to which service.
tldr.mechanism: LoST Sync defines XML messages over HTTPS: a destination can pull mappings with getMappingsRequest, and a source can push new, updated or deleted mappings with pushMappingsRequest.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental protocol. Mappings must be signed with XML digital signatures, and the RFC has been updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 6739 is an Experimental RFC and has been updated by RFC 8996. Check that update for what changed.

sections.title: What LoST Sync Does
sections.content:
The LoST protocol (RFC 5222) maps a service identifier and a location to service URIs and service boundaries. A service boundary circumscribes the region within which all locations map to the same service URI or set of URIs, and it may consist of several non-contiguous shapes. The data structure that carries it is the <mapping> element.

RFC 6739 reuses that element and defines an XML protocol, called LoST Sync, to exchange authoritative mappings between two entities: the LoST Sync source and the LoST Sync destination. It can be used whether or not LoST itself is used for queries. Exchanging cached, non-authoritative mappings is possible but not envisioned.
sections.eli5: Each emergency map says which call center answers for which area. This protocol is how two computers swap those maps so they stay in step.

sections.title: A Motivating Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC builds an example on the mapping architecture of RFC 5582. LoST servers peer with each other, peering is set up manually based on local policy, and authoritative mapping servers push their coverage regions up the tree to parent nodes, such as forest guides.

In the hypothetical example, Austria has three authoritative servers (East, West and Vienna) that report to an Austrian forest guide, while Finland runs one LoST server co-located with its forest guide. LoST Sync would run between the two forest guides and between the Austrian servers and their forest guide. Because the data volume is small and changes are rare, the example nodes simply exchange all of their mappings whenever a change happens.

The RFC does not define a publish/subscribe mechanism, nor a way for nodes to find out to which entities mappings should be pushed.
sections.eli5: Think of town offices sending their updated maps up to a regional office, and regional offices swapping maps with each other.

sections.title: Pulling and Pushing Mappings
sections.content:
There are two exchanges. In the pull, the destination sends <getMappingsRequest> to the source and gets a <getMappingsResponse>. An empty request asks for all mappings, and the source MUST then return all it has. A request with one or more <exists> children lists mappings the destination already has, so the source returns only missing or newer ones. A newer mapping is found by matching the source and sourceId attributes and comparing lastUpdated.

In the push, the source sends <pushMappingsRequest> with one or more <mapping> elements and the destination answers with <pushMappingsResponse>. A mapping is considered the same if source, sourceId and lastUpdated match. The source SHOULD keep track of what it has pushed to whom; otherwise it must push the full data set.

To delete, the source sends a <mapping> that has only the source, sourceId, lastUpdated and expires attributes; expires is required by the schema but ignored. If the destination cannot find the mapping, it MUST return an <errors> response with a <notDeleted> element.
sections.eli5: You can ask a friend, "send me every map you have," or "send me only the ones that changed since mine." Or the friend can call you and say, "here are new ones, and throw this old one away."

sections.title: Transport and Roles
sections.content:
LoST Sync carries its XML over HTTPS, with no fallback to plain HTTP. Messages use the POST method, and requests MUST use the Cache-Control directive no-cache. All LoST Sync responses, including errors and warnings, travel in 2xx responses, typically 200. HTTP 3xx, 4xx and 5xx codes mean the request itself failed or was redirected, and carry no LoST Sync XML.

Whichever side sends the first request is the HTTPS client. In a pull, the destination is the client; in a push, the source is the client. Only some LoST errors are reused: <badRequest>, <forbidden>, <internalError> and <serverTimeout>, while <redirect> and <warnings> are not used. The RFC also includes a RELAX NG schema for the messages.
sections.eli5: The messages ride inside ordinary secure web requests, and whoever starts the conversation plays the asker.

sections.title: Loops, Signing and Security
sections.content:
With more than two peers, loops are a concern: if servers A, B and C all sync with each other, a new mapping could circulate. Because a mapping is identified by source, sourceId and lastUpdated, a server that already has an unmodified copy can ignore it. Implementations MUST NOT modify mappings they receive.

To stop an untrustworthy member from claiming a region it does not own, authoritative servers MUST sign the mappings they distribute with an XML digital signature, and the recipient MUST verify that the signer is authorized to speak for that region. The client and servers MUST implement and use TLS. Mutual authentication is not necessarily required unless an authority wants access control. The RFC warns that injected mappings could cause denial of service, overload a single PSAP, or point to a server that impersonates PSAPs.
sections.eli5: Every map gets a signature, like a stamp from the real map-maker, so nobody can slip in a fake map that sends emergency calls to the wrong place.
